data.rationale: Tile the M-dimension (i) with factor 64. A 64-row tile per thread-block is a standard choice for Ampere GEMM — it keeps each CTA working on a 64×64 output tile, giving enough reuse to amortize shared-memory loads while keeping register pressure manageable. 256/64 = 4 tiles along M, which distributes well across 30 SMs.

Tile the N-dimension (j) with factor 64 to match the i-tile. A symmetric 64×64 output tile per CTA is the textbook blocked-GEMM configuration: both A-tile (64×k_tile) and B-tile (k_tile×64) fit in the 49KB shared memory, maximises data reuse on both operands, and produces a square output tile that maps cleanly to warp-level MMA layouts on Ampere.

Tile the K-reduction axis with factor 16. A k-tile of 16 means each iteration loads a 64×16 slice of A and a 16×64 slice of B into shared memory (64×16 + 16×64 = 2048 fp32 elements = 8KB, well within 49KB), then accumulates into the 64×64 register tile. 16 steps of 16 across the K=256 dimension gives 16 pipelineable stages — small enough to hide latency without over-subscribing registers.

Switch to a 32-row tile on i. For a 256×256 problem, 64×64 tiles yielded only 16 CTAs (under-utilizing 30 SMs). With tile=32 on both i and j we get 8×8=64 CTAs, spreading work across all 30 SMs with ~2 waves, far better occupancy than the 64-based strategy.

Symmetric 32-column tile on j to pair with the 32-row i-tile. The 32×32 output tile fits cleanly within warp-level MMA fragments on Ampere and keeps the shared-memory footprint (32×16 + 16×32 = 1024 fp32 = 4KB) well within 49KB budget, leaving headroom for double-buffering later.
